unit.title: Communicate information relating to work activities

summary: This unit teaches you to gather, check and pass on information about work activities so that the right people have the right facts at the right time. You will learn to write clear reports and instructions, present figures in tables and charts, give briefings and handovers, choose the best channel for each message, keep orderly records and files, protect confidential information, write incident reports and pass problems and suggestions up to management.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Work runs on information: how many orders were processed, what the new procedure is, who is on shift, what went wrong, what a customer was promised. When information is late, wrong or does not reach the right person, mistakes follow, such as double orders, missed deliveries, safety incidents and unhappy customers.

As a supervisor or manager you are the link between the people doing the work and those who decide. You collect information from the team, check it, pass it up in a useful form, and pass decisions and instructions back down so that people can act on them.
**Who it is for:** supervisors, team leaders and managers in any workplace: offices, warehouses, hotels, schools, health services, call centres and public bodies.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Take figures from work records and systems, check them against the source, and organise them.
Use clear headings, put the main points first, show results against targets and suggest actions.
Use tables, charts, averages and percentages so that readers can act.
Write procedures as numbered steps, brief the team and check that they understand.
Use the right medium for urgent, routine, formal and private messages.
Fill in forms correctly, name and store files properly, keep records for the required time and protect personal data.
Report incidents factually, escalate problems at the right time and forward suggestions.
Find where information fails and fix it.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios and calculations.
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms and quick sums) and longer answers.
**Group practicals**: compiling and presenting a weekly work activity report, and writing a work procedure, briefing a team and recording feedback. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Check every figure twice before you pass it on. A wrong number in a report travels a long way.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Source
Examples
Check
rows: Output sheets, order logs, timesheets, attendance, stock records
Reports from the accounting, stock, booking or call-centre system
Were the right dates and filters used?
What you see on the floor; what team members tell you
Is it a pattern or a one-off?

blocks.note: Take figures **from the source records and system reports**, not from memory or from someone's summary.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Check before you pass it on

flow: Check the figures against the source records
Re-add the totals, and recalculate percentages and averages
Make sure the dates and units are right
Mark what is a fact and what is an estimate or opinion
Ask someone else to read it if it is important

ul: Start with the **purpose**: what does the reader need to know or decide?
Group the information under clear headings (for example output, quality, attendance, safety, issues).
Put the **main points first**, then the detail.
Give figures with their units and the period they cover.
Keep opinions apart from facts, and say what you recommend.

head: Fact (can be checked)
Opinion (a view)
rows: The spill was 1 metre from the door.
The printer failed at 9:15 a.m. and was repaired at 11:00 a.m.

blocks.p: Use facts in reports and incident records. If you give an opinion, label it as one and say what the facts are behind it.

head: Part
Content
rows: The main points in two or three lines, including what you need from the reader
Actual figures beside targets, with the gap
What went wrong or well, and why
What is being done, by whom, by when; what you recommend

blocks.p: If a manager asks for a one-page update on overtime, include the **overtime hours, the causes and suggested actions**. Use clear headings and put the main points first. A report that the manager can read in two minutes and act on is better than a long one that hides the point.
Readers should see at once whether the team is ahead or behind. Put **actual results beside the targets** and show the gap or percentage.

head: Measure
Formula
Worked example
rows: Orders over five days: 160, 152, 148, 170, 170 = 800 ÷ 5 = 160 a day
Complaints from 40 to 30 is a 25% fall
360 calls in 8 hours = 45 calls per hour

head: Purpose
Best format
rows: Exact figures for 4 shifts over 5 days
A table, with shifts as rows and days as columns
Output over the last six months
The parts of a whole (share of calls by type)
A pie chart, with few slices
A short table, then one chart for the key message

blocks.p: Give every table and chart a **title that says what it shows**, label the units, name the source and the period, and keep one message to each chart.

If a weekly report is due at 10:00 a.m. each Monday and the data is ready at 9:00 a.m., a **report template** with the headings, tables and charts already set up lets the supervisor finish in time and makes each week's report comparable.

A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is a written, step-by-step method for a routine task. It makes sure that the task is done the **same safe way each time**, whoever does it, and helps new staff learn.

head: Part of an SOP
What it holds
rows: What the task is and why it matters
Who does it and when it applies
What is needed, including forms and log sheets
Numbered, in the order they are done, one action in each
What to check, and any safety or privacy points
What to do if it goes wrong
Who to call or what to do next
So that everyone uses the current copy

ul: Use **numbered steps** in the order they are done.
Start each step with a verb: *Check*, *Enter*, *Send*.
Be specific: "Send the form to Accounts by Friday noon" is clearer than "Send it soon".
One action per step; short sentences.
Say who does what and by when.
Use a diagram or checklist where it helps.

flow: Explain why the change is needed and what it is
Take the team through the steps, showing where possible
Let each person try a step (a trial run)
Ask questions to check understanding, such as "Show me what you would do if..."
Note questions and feedback, and update the procedure if needed

blocks.note: Asking a new clerk to **explain the steps back in her own words**, or to try them, is better than asking "Do you understand?" People often say yes when they do not.
blocks.label: Tip

ol: Update the procedure, with a new version number and date.
Remove the old copy from use, on paper and in shared folders.
Brief the team and check understanding.
Give those affected the written copy and answer questions.
Check after a few weeks that it is being used.

blocks.p: A **briefing** is a short, regular meeting in which the supervisor passes on information before work begins: for example the day's arrivals, tasks, issues and safety points. A **handover** passes work information from one shift or person to the next.

ul: Work in progress and what has been done
Open issues and who is dealing with them
Anything urgent or unusual (a VIP guest, a broken machine, a promise made to a customer)
Safety or security concerns
What the next person needs to do first

blocks.p: Use a written **handover log** as well as a spoken handover. If the information exists only in someone's head, it leaves when they do.

ul: For a team member whose first language is not English: short sentences, show the steps, avoid slang and check understanding.
For a member with a visual impairment: provide information in a format she can use, such as large print, an audio version or a screen-reader-friendly file.
For someone who reads slowly or has dyslexia: use plain layouts, clear fonts, short lists, and talk it through.
Ask each person what works best for them.

head: Channel
Best for
Not good for
rows: Explaining changes, checking understanding, sensitive or complex matters
Messages that must be kept as a record
Urgent matters, quick answers, closing the office suddenly
Detail that must be recorded (follow up in writing)
Urgent alerts to many people, quick reminders
Formal messages, detailed information, records, attachments
Rotas, duties, reminders, information for all to see

blocks.p: **Match the message to the channel.** A burst water main that forces the office to close is urgent: tell staff first by a direct call or group alert. A fire drill tomorrow at 10:00 a.m. is best given by a team message and a notice on the board, so that people see it twice. A new rota for canteen duties belongs on the staff notice board.

blocks.note: If a manager gives you an urgent instruction by phone that changes a delivery, **confirm it by email and note it in the log**. Spoken instructions are easily misremembered.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Write a **clear subject line** that says what it is about: "Stock count results – Store 2, 14 March".
Open with the main point or request, then give the detail.
Say what you need, from whom and by when.
Keep it short; one subject per email.
Check names, dates and attachments before you send.
Do not put private or confidential data in a general group.
Keep to **work topics** and share no private data.
Agree which channel is for which kind of message, so people do not get too many emails or messages and miss the important ones.
Do not use a group to criticise individuals.
Remember that a message may be shared or kept as a record.

blocks.p: Take notes, repeat the key points back ("So I am to move the delivery to Thursday, and tell the driver today") and confirm any change in writing. Ask if anything is unclear.

When you complete a form, fill in **every required field clearly and correctly**: dates, names, quantities and signatures. An incomplete form may have to be redone, delay work or cause a dispute. Use the form as the standard record, and keep it where it can be found.

ul: Use a **clear naming rule** with the topic, the date and the version: for example *Overtime-Dispatch-2026-03-v2*.
Do not use names such as "report1" or "final final".
Keep the current versions in a shared folder that the team can open; move old versions to an archive.
Use **one shared master file** with a version history where several people edit the same rota or document, so that changes are not lost or overwritten.
Keep paper files in labelled folders, in an order that makes sense (by date, name or number), in a lockable cabinet.
Back up important computer files.

head: Belongs in a shared team folder
Does not

blocks.p: Keep work records, such as timesheets, **for the period set by policy and the law**, and then dispose of them securely (shredding or secure deletion).

The data protection law in Jamaica sets general rules for personal data: collect only what you need, use it only for its purpose, keep it accurate and secure, and limit who can see it. Customers' and staff members' personal information is confidential.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A colleague asks for another employee's home address
Refuse and follow the privacy policy; offer to pass on a message
A team keeps a spreadsheet of clients' phone numbers
Limit access, use it only for its purpose, and keep it secure
An employee gives a supervisor a medical certificate
Share only with those who need it (for example HR), not with the whole team
Customer details are wanted on a personal phone
Use only approved systems; do not copy data to personal devices or private chats

blocks.note: Before discussing personal information, ask: *does this person need to know?* If not, do not share it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: If a team member privately reports a possible fraud, **do not investigate or confront anyone yourself**. Listen, write down the facts, keep the matter private and report it through the proper channel (for example your manager, internal audit or the confidential reporting line), as the organisation's policy says.

sections.title: Passing information up: incidents, problems and suggestions

blocks.p: An **incident report** is a written record of an accident or near miss. Complete it as soon as possible after first aid and making the area safe.

head: Include
Example
rows: Name, role, date, time and exact place
The worker slipped on a wet floor in the store room at 2:10 p.m.
First aid given; area cordoned off; manager informed
A leak from the roof was running onto the floor
Repair the roof; fit a warning sign; check the other rooms

blocks.note: Write facts, such as "The spill was 1 metre from the door", and keep opinions out. Do not blame; describe. Your report may be used for insurance, investigation or legal purposes.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Escalation** means passing a problem you cannot solve at your level to a higher authority. When a supplier's delay will stop production in two days, tell your manager at once, with the facts and the options, rather than waiting.

flow: Describe the problem in a sentence
Give the key facts and figures
Say what the effect will be and when
Say what you have already done
Ask for the decision or help you need, and by when

blocks.p: When you give a quick spoken update, give the **main point, the key figures and what you need**.

ul: If team members say that a new form takes too long to fill in, **collect examples** and pass them on with suggestions.
Thank staff for suggestions, even if they are not practical; explain the limits and invite other ideas.
Tell the team what happened to their suggestion.
Keep a log of suggestions and replies.

blocks.p: Ask the team, and **trace errors back to poor information**: where was it late, unclear, missing or sent to the wrong person? Common causes and fixes:

head: Cause of the problem
Improvement
rows: Information given only by word of mouth
Agree which channel is for which kind of message
A handover log and a short briefing
Staff do not know why a change was made
Explain the reason when you brief
One shared master file with version control

ul: gather figures from source records and system reports, and check them before passing them on
separate facts from opinions
organise a short report with clear headings and the main points first
show results beside targets and calculate averages, percentages, percentage change and rates, checking each twice
choose a table, column, line, bar or pie chart to suit the data
write procedures as numbered steps and brief a team, checking understanding
run a briefing and a handover with a written log
choose the best channel for urgent, routine and formal messages, and confirm phone instructions in writing
write clear email subject lines and keep team chats to work topics
name, store and version files, and keep records for the required time
protect confidential and personal information
write a factual incident report
escalate problems and pass on suggestions properly
find and fix the causes of poor information flow

terms: Standard operating procedure: a written, step-by-step method for a routine task
Key performance indicator: a measure used to track progress toward a target
Passing work information from one shift or person to the next
A short, regular meeting to pass on information before work starts
A written record of an accident or near miss
A document that gives facts, findings and recommendations on a work matter
Passing a problem you cannot solve to a higher authority
Information that may be shared only with authorised people
Keeping track of changes to a document, for example v1, v2 and v3
The short title line of an email
A ready-made layout for a report or form
A document that lists who works which shift on which day
A dated record of events or actions
A statement that can be checked
The total divided by the number of values
The change as a percentage of the old figure
A chart of slices of a circle that show the parts of a whole
Rules for keeping personal information safe and using it fairly
Keeping records for the required period and then disposing of them securely

c1.title: The weekly report of an orders section
c1.text: Opal Clarke supervises the orders section of a distributor in Mandeville. Orders processed this week from Monday to Friday were 160, 152, 148, 170 and 170. The weekly target was 1,000 orders. Errors logged were 30 last week and 24 this week. Her manager wants the report by 10:00 on Monday, and the system data is ready at 9:00.

c2.title: A shift handover at an Ocho Rios resort
c2.text: The evening receptionist at a resort in Ocho Rios finished her shift and left without logging that a guest in Room 14 had been promised a late checkout and that the air conditioner in Room 22 was leaking. The morning receptionist, Jerome, found out at 11:30 a.m., when the guest complained that housekeeping had entered the room.

c3.title: A new fee receipt procedure at a high school
c3.text: Mrs Hylton, the bursar of a high school in St Ann, introduces a new procedure for issuing fee receipts. Two clerks, one of whom reads slowly because of dyslexia, must follow it. The old procedure is saved in the shared folder as 'receipts final final'.

c4.title: Confidential information at a security company
c4.text: Everton Powell supervises guards at a security company in Portmore. A guard gives him a medical certificate. Another guard posts a client's alarm code in the team's WhatsApp group by mistake. At 6:00 p.m. the operations manager phones to say that tomorrow's patrol schedule at one client's site has changed.

c5.title: An accident in a warehouse in Portmore
c5.text: A worker slips on a wet floor near a loading bay of a warehouse in Portmore at 2:10 p.m. After first aid, supervisor Camille Bryan must complete the incident report. A leak from the roof has been running onto the floor for two weeks. Camille cannot repair the roof herself, and the maintenance budget is controlled by the facilities manager.

questions.q: What was the average number of orders processed per day this week?
What percentage of the weekly target was reached?
questions.why: 800 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 80%. The base is the target. Check: 80% of 1,000 = 800.

questions.q: By what percentage did errors fall from last week to this week?
questions.why: (30 − 24) ÷ 30 × 100 = 6 ÷ 30 × 100 = 20%. The base is last week's figure. Check: 20% of 30 = 6, and 30 − 6 = 24.

questions.q: What should Opal do so that the report is ready by 10:00?
o: Wait for the data, then write the whole report from a blank page
Prepare a report template and fill it in when data arrives
Send the manager the raw data so that she can work it out herself
Leave out the check of the totals so that the report is on time
questions.why: A template with headings, tables and charts already prepared lets her finish quickly and makes each week's report comparable. Checking the totals must never be skipped.

questions.q: Which presentation shows the daily output for the five days most clearly?
o: A column chart with a bar for each day
A pie chart with a slice for each day
A paragraph that lists the five numbers
A chart showing only the weekly total
questions.why: Comparing amounts for each day is best shown with columns or a line. A pie chart suits parts of a whole, and a total hides the daily pattern.

questions.q: What was the main failing in the receptionist's handover?
o: She finished her shift earlier than she should have done
She spoke too quietly when she told the other manager
She completed too many forms before she left the desk
Urgent items and promises were not logged for the next shift
questions.why: A handover must include work in progress, open issues and anything urgent or promised. Without a log, the important information left with her.

questions.q: What should Jerome do first about Room 14 after the complaint?
o: Tell the guest that the mistake was not his fault
Blame the evening receptionist in front of the guest
Apologise, check the facts and put it right for the guest
Say nothing, so as not to draw more attention to it
questions.why: The guest comes first: apologise, check the facts and fix the problem. The handover failure can be dealt with afterwards, in private.

questions.q: Which change will best prevent this from happening again?
o: A rule that no one may leave the desk until midnight
A notice reminding staff to try to remember everything
A written handover log completed at every shift change
Taking the late checkout service away from guests
questions.why: A written log makes the handover reliable. Relying on memory, or removing a service, does not fix the flow of information.

questions.q: Mrs Hylton is writing the new receipt procedure. How should she lay it out?
o: As one long paragraph containing all the details
As numbered steps in the order they are done
As a list of rules in alphabetical order
As a table that lists the clerks by name
questions.why: Numbered steps in order, one action in each, make a procedure easy to follow and to check.

questions.q: What is the best way to confirm that the clerks understand the new procedure?
o: Ask them to try the steps and explain them back
Ask whether they have any questions at the end
Send them the document by email and wait
Tell them it is their job to read it carefully
questions.why: A trial run and teach-back show what people can actually do. Asking "Any questions?" often brings silence even when people are unsure.

questions.q: The clerk who reads slowly is given the procedure. What helps most?
o: A long paragraph of text set in very small type
No written copy, only a spoken explanation on the day
A different procedure that has fewer checks in it
Short numbered steps in plain layout, talked through
questions.why: A plain layout, short steps and a talk-through support the clerk without lowering the standard she must meet. Removing the written copy would take away her reference.

questions.q: What should happen to the old file 'receipts final final'?
o: Leave it in the shared folder in case someone wants it
Rename it 'receipts final final 2' and keep it there too
Keep both versions and let each clerk choose between them
Remove it and replace it with a clearly named, dated version
questions.why: Two live versions cause errors. Remove or archive the old copy and use a clear name with a date and version number.

questions.q: Everton is given a guard's medical certificate. What should he do with it?
o: Show it to the whole team to explain the absence
Post a copy of it in the team chat group
Share it only with those who need it, such as HR
Pin it on the notice board in the guardroom
questions.why: Medical information is confidential. Only those who need it, such as HR, should see it.

questions.q: A guard has posted a client's alarm code in the WhatsApp group. What should Everton do?
o: Ignore it, since only guards are in the group
Have it deleted, report it, and set chat rules
Ask the group to memorise the code and move on
Leave it for a week to see if anyone complains
questions.why: A client's security data must not sit in an open chat. Delete it, report it so that the code can be changed, and set clear rules about what may be shared in chat.

questions.q: The operations manager phones at 6:00 p.m. about a schedule change for tomorrow. What should Everton do?
o: Take notes, repeat the details back and confirm in writing
Rely on memory and tell the guards in the morning
Wait until a written notice is delivered to the site
Ask one guard to pass the news to the rest
questions.why: Spoken instructions are easily misremembered. Note them, read them back, confirm in writing and tell the guards in good time.

questions.q: Which way is best for telling the guards tonight about tomorrow's changed schedule?
o: Contact each guard directly and post an updated rota
Put a notice on the board for the guards to see next week
Send an email about it to the client's office
Add a comment to the general chat and hope it is read
questions.why: The message is urgent and must reach every guard. Direct contact and an updated rota make the change certain and recorded.

questions.q: Which sentence is suitable for Camille's incident report?
o: The worker was careless and did not look where he was going
The warehouse is dangerous because of poor management of the site
The floor was probably wet because someone was too lazy to mop
The worker slipped on a wet floor near the loading bay at 2:10 p.m.
questions.why: An incident report records facts that can be checked: time, place and what happened. Opinions and blame are left out.

questions.q: Camille cannot repair the roof leak. What is the best next step?
o: Wait until someone else mentions the leak to the manager
Tell the workers to keep away from the area for good
Report the hazard to the facilities manager, with the facts
Mop the floor each day and say nothing to anyone
questions.why: Escalate a problem you cannot solve, with the facts, the risk and your suggestion. A warning sign and cleaning can be used meanwhile, but the manager must know.

questions.q: Why does the report also record the cause and the actions to prevent a repeat?
o: So that the worker can be disciplined for the accident
So the cause can be fixed and the report used for follow-up
So that the report looks longer and more serious
So that the manager does not have to read the rest
questions.why: Incident reports are used to find causes and stop repeats. Their purpose is safety and learning, not blame.

questions.q: This month's calls were 40% billing, 30% delivery, 20% product and 10% other. Which chart shows these shares of the whole best?
o: A line graph with four points
A pie chart with four slices
A table in alphabetical order of call type
A chart that shows only the billing calls
questions.why: A pie chart shows how parts make up a whole, and four slices are few enough to read easily. A line graph is for change over time.
